title: Control of purple nutsedge in perennial crop fields - Vietnam

Header: Control of purple nutsedge in perennial crop fields - Vietnam
Cyperus rotundus Cỏgấu, Hương phụ, Cỏcú

Prevention: Prevention is particularly important as the weed is difficult to control.
Seeds are considered unimportant; tubers are the main means of spread.
Clean tools and farm machinery to prevent tubers from being spread.
Do not accept potentially contaminated materials, e.g. soil on planting stock.
Control established populations near waterways to prevent spread during flooding and storm events.
Monitoring: Additional relevant crops: perennial crops such as citrus, litchi, longan, and mango.
Erect, perennial sedge (30-60cm high), with extensive underground network composed of tubers.
Tubers dark brown/black, irregularly shaped, 1-2cm long at maturity, with several buds.
Leaves linear with distinct midrib, 7mm wide.
Inflorescence with several unequal 'branches', each 2-6cm long, emerging from the tip of the stem; each with 3-8 purplish-brown flowerheads.
Inspect fields monthly, in particular during and shortly after the wet season, and consider direct control when weed is found.
Look our for it in wetlands and along waterways.
Water and storm events can spread tubers.
Direct Control: Tubers and rhizomes in the soil can be destroyed by desiccation (most effective in dry soil) or exhausting food reserves.
Cultivate every 2-3 weeks until crop canopy forms: the weed is shade intolerant.
Place organic mulch over areas where weed is expected to grow: provides temporary suppression.
Tillage must be deep (>12cm) to disturb as many of the rhizomes as possible.
Do this under dry conditions so the exposed rhizomes desiccate.
Tillage should be done three times weekly.
Restrictions: Use of chemical herbicides may lead to the development of herbicide resistance.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage
Few herbicides kill the weed, but some can be used to suppress weed until crop canopy closes.
Studies have reported resistance against some pesticides.
The most effective herbicide is glyphosate.
Apply at a rate of 1500-2000g a.i/ha at the post-emergence state of the weed but before the flowering stage.
